title: Goldman's CEO Told This Summer's Interns to Spar With the AI
author: Mike Kentz
summary: Mike Kentz builds an argument around a specific instruction Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon reportedly gave incoming interns: not to avoid AI and not to defer to it uncritically, but to 'spar' with it, treating model output the way you'd treat a smart, occasionally wrong colleague worth actively arguing with. Kentz argues this single word captures a posture missing from nearly all K-12 and higher-ed AI guidance, which he sorts into two camps, avoidance framing that treats AI as making students weaker, and uncritical-use framing that treats AI as just a tool to learn to operate, both of which he argues position the student as fundamentally passive relative to the model. His central claim is that sparring requires students to already have enough developing expertise to notice when AI output is off and enough intellectual confidence to push back, which neither avoidance nor deference training actually builds. He proposes a concrete classroom translation: after receiving AI-generated output, students must find and argue, with evidence, against one thing in it they think is wrong or incomplete, not because AI is usually badly wrong, but because hunting for the weak point in someone else's argument is itself a durable intellectual skill.
points: Anchors the argument in Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon's reported instruction to interns to 'spar' with AI output rather than avoid or defer to it, arguing that single word captures a posture missing from most school AI guidance.
Sorts existing classroom AI policy into two camps, avoidance and uncritical use, arguing both treat the student's relationship to the model as fundamentally passive rather than active and reciprocal.

Argues sparring specifically requires students to already possess enough developing expertise to notice flawed AI output and enough intellectual confidence to push back, a prerequisite neither avoidance nor deference training builds.

Translates the metaphor into a concrete classroom practice: after AI output, students must identify and argue against one specific weak point with evidence, framed as building the durable skill of hunting for weaknesses in any argument, not just AI's.
quotes: He didn't tell them to avoid AI, and he didn't tell them to use it uncritically either. He told them to spar with it.
Spar implies engagement, not avoidance and not surrender. A boxer sparring with a partner isn't refusing to throw punches, and isn't just standing there absorbing them either.
Camp one wants students passively avoiding the tool. Camp two wants students passively deferring to it once they've learned to operate it. Sparring is neither.
Sparring requires the student to have enough of their own developing expertise to notice when the AI's output is off, and enough intellectual confidence to say so and push back.
The next required step is: find one thing in this output you think is wrong, incomplete, or could be argued with, and make that argument, with evidence, in your own words.
The discipline of actively hunting for the weak point in someone else's argument, even a very good one, is itself one of the most durable intellectual skills there is.
